content:
Alcohol and arthritis is a topic that causes confusion. Can you still enjoy a drink? Does alcohol make arthritis worse? And what about interactions with your medication? Here's what the evidence says.

Quick answer: Moderate alcohol consumption may slightly reduce rheumatoid arthritis risk but can also worsen inflammation, gout, and sleep. Alcohol interacts with many arthritis medications: combining it with methotrexate increases liver damage risk, and with NSAIDs or steroids, it raises stomach ulcer risk. The NHS recommends no more than 14 units per week. Discuss alcohol intake with your rheumatologist.

How Alcohol Affects Arthritis

Potential Benefits (in Moderation)

Some studies suggest that moderate alcohol consumption may slightly reduce the risk of developing rheumatoid arthritis, possibly through anti-inflammatory effects. However, this doesn't mean alcohol is recommended as a health measure.

Potential Harms

  • Inflammation — heavy drinking increases systemic inflammation
  • Weight gain — alcohol is calorie-dense, contributing to weight that stresses joints
  • Gout — alcohol (especially beer and spirits) is a major trigger for gout attacks
  • Sleep disruption — alcohol impairs sleep quality, worsening fatigue and pain
  • Bone health — heavy drinking reduces bone density, increasing fracture risk

Medication Interactions

Methotrexate

This is the most important interaction. Methotrexate and alcohol are both processed by the liver. Combining them increases the risk of liver damage. Current UK guidance from the BSR (British Society for Rheumatology) advises:

  • Stay within NHS guidelines (14 units per week maximum)
  • Some rheumatologists recommend lower limits or complete abstinence
  • Discuss your individual risk with your rheumatologist
  • Regular liver blood tests are essential while on methotrexate

NSAIDs (Ibuprofen, Naproxen)

Alcohol combined with NSAIDs increases the risk of stomach bleeding and ulcers. If you take regular NSAIDs, limit alcohol carefully.

Steroids (Prednisolone)

Both steroids and alcohol can irritate the stomach lining. Combining them increases ulcer risk.

UK Alcohol Guidelines

The NHS recommends no more than 14 units per week, spread across 3 or more days. For context:

  • 1 pint of beer/cider = 2-3 units
  • 1 glass of wine (175ml) = 2 units
  • 1 single spirit (25ml) = 1 unit

Practical Tips

  • Have several alcohol-free days per week
  • Choose lower-strength drinks when you do drink
  • Alternate alcoholic drinks with water
  • If you have gout, avoid beer entirely and limit all alcohol
  • Be honest with your rheumatologist about your alcohol consumption

Everyone's situation is different. Discuss alcohol with your rheumatologist, especially if you take methotrexate or other liver-processed medications.

Practical next steps for Arthritis and Alcohol – What You Need to Know

If you came here about Arthritis and Alcohol – What You Need to Know, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your NHS trust about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Cross-check major decisions with NHS.uk, your clinical team, and NICE guidance summaries where relevant. Be wary of social posts that promise reversal of arthritis or attack standard medicines without evidence.

Peer support etiquette

Share what helps you without prescribing it for others. Conditions, medicines and life circumstances differ. If someone is in crisis, encourage them toward NHS 111, their GP, or emergency services rather than relying on a forum alone.

Quick questions about Arthritis Alcohol What Need

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.
